in_context.text: Paul is answering false teachers who forbade marriage and told believers to avoid certain foods (4:1-3). He replies that everything God made is good. Nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanks, because it is set apart by God's word and prayer (4:5).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself at the start of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in Paul's name; others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus. Paul wants him to remind the believers of these things (4:6).

affected.text: Believers who were being told to give up marriage and certain foods. The false teachers who taught those rules are also in view.

what.text: The verse explains why the ban on marriage and foods is wrong. God created these things to be received with thanksgiving, and every created thing of God is good. None of it is to be thrown away when it is received gratefully.

events.text: Paul says the Spirit warned that in the latter times some would leave the faith and teach such rules. He treats this teaching as already a danger Timothy must face.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: The letter was sent to Timothy in Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Where it was written from is not stated, though it may have been Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul wants to expose a false, strict teaching and give Timothy a clear answer to it. That answer is the goodness of God's creation, received with thanks.

big_picture.text: The verse echoes creation, where God saw everything he had made as very good. Elsewhere Paul likewise teaches that no food is unclean of itself.

for_readers.text: Ordinary gifts like food and marriage are not spiritually suspect in themselves. Readers are invited to receive them with thankfulness and prayer rather than fear.

misuse.popular_reading: Quoted as blanket approval of anything a person wants, as if "nothing to be refused" means no limits on any behavior or substance.

in_context_reading.text: The verse answers a specific false teaching that banned marriage and foods (4:3). It speaks of things God created, received with thanksgiving and set apart by God's word and prayer. Paul elsewhere notes that not all lawful things are helpful.

why_it_matters.text: The Greek means "a created thing," not only an animal. Paul is speaking of what God made, such as the foods and marriage mentioned in 4:3.
The word means "to be thrown away" or rejected. Paul is denying that God's good gifts should be cast aside as unholy.
The word means giving thanks or gratitude. The condition in the verse is a grateful heart toward God, not a list of banned items.

takeaway.text: God's created gifts are good. They are to be received with thanks, not rejected by man-made rules that call them unholy.

resolved.reason: The cited verses say nothing about Protestant, Catholic, or Orthodox positions on clerical celibacy, fasting disciplines, or Old Testament food laws. These views of later traditions are not in any cited source.
resolved.fix: note removed at Kourtland's direction: the verse plainly says everything God created is good
